questions.question: Which three properties define an equivalence relation?
For an equivalence relation, any two equivalence classes are either:
If $a\sim b$ under an equivalence relation, then the classes $[a]$ and $[b]$ are:
Under an equivalence relation on $A$, each element of $A$ belongs to:
What is the interpretation of an equivalence relation?
options: It counts the number of elements in a set
It orders objects from smallest to largest
It says when different objects count as the same

questions.question: On the integers, the relation “has the same parity as” is an equivalence relation. Which property explains why every integer has the same parity as itself?
For congruence modulo $3$, is $4\sim10$?
options: Yes, because $4$ and $10$ have the same remainder modulo $3$
No, because congruence modulo $3$ is not an equivalence relation
Yes, because all integers are congruent modulo $3$

questions.question: Which relation on real numbers is not an equivalence relation?
Equal cardinality of sets is an equivalence relation. What proves the symmetric part?
options: The empty set has one element
The inverse of a bijection is a bijection
Every set has larger power set

questions.question: If $a\sim b$ and $b\sim c$ imply $a\sim c$, which property is being used?
Why is symmetry not the same as reflexivity?
options: Reflexivity says every relation can be reversed
Symmetry is between two objects; reflexivity is an object with itself
The two words always describe identical conditions, which is false
Symmetry says every object is related to itself

questions.question: Why is transitivity important when equivalence is meant to represent “same for this purpose”?
options: It prevents chains of sameness from breaking at the endpoints
It says unrelated objects must become related
It forces every equivalence class to contain one element
It says $a\sim b$ can hold only when $a=b$

questions.question: How does equal cardinality fit the idea of an equivalence relation?
options: Sets with a bijection between them are treated as having the same size
Sets with equal cardinality must contain exactly the same elements
Equal cardinality means both sets are finite
Equal cardinality gives a linear order of all sets

questions.question: For the relation $a\sim b$ iff $a-b$ is divisible by $5$, which statement is true?
On real numbers, let $a\sim b$ mean $|a|=|b|$. Which number is equivalent to $-3$?
The relation $a\le b$ on real numbers fails to be an equivalence relation mainly because which property fails?
What larger structure is usually produced by an equivalence relation on a set?
options: A total order with a unique maximum
A determinant for every pair of elements
A power set with no empty subset

questions.question: Why does equal cardinality use composition of bijections for transitivity?
options: Composition of bijections is never a bijection, which is false
If $A$ matches $B$ and $B$ matches $C$, the composition pairs $A$ with $C$
Transitivity requires only that $A=B=C$ as sets

questions.question: Under congruence modulo $4$, which numbers lie in the same equivalence class as $1$?
A relation satisfies reflexivity and symmetry, but there are $a,b,c$ with $a\sim b$ and $b\sim c$ while $a\not\sim c$. What can be concluded?
options: It is not an equivalence relation because transitivity fails
It is an equivalence relation because two properties are enough
